## Paper

## Abstract

The Global Carbon Project (GCP) compiles an updated global carbon budget each year, synthesizing state-of-the-art estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions, land and ocean sinks, and the atmospheric CO2 growth rate. The residual between these terms, referred to as the global carbon budget imbalance, reflects the aggregate inaccuracies of the individual component estimates. Growth rates derived from marine boundary layer (MBL) surface flask mixing ratio observations are assumed to be highly accurate. Hence, land and ocean sink estimates from process models are viewed as the primary source of the imbalance. Here we show that substantial discrepancies arise when marine boundary layer growth rate estimates are used to represent the whole atmosphere. Correcting for this discrepancy using atmospheric flux inversion estimates reduces the 0.76 petagrams of carbon per year (PgC yr−1) root-mean-square (RMS) imbalance (from the 2023 GCP report) by up to 25%. Further investigation into the imbalance metric between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports shows a reduction in imbalance resulting from updates to each carbon budget component, leading to a 16% overall reduction. These reductions provide quantitative evidence of improvements in process models and inventory emission estimates, driven by enhanced forcing data and the inclusion of new carbon cycle processes. Overall, we report a 37% reduction in the root-mean-square imbalance, from 0.91 to 0.57 PgC yr−1, between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports by combining process model and inventory improvements with atmospheric growth rate corrections. Our findings indicate that land and ocean process models are more accurate than previously believed and that the scientific understanding of Earth’s carbon cycle is improving.

---

## Introduction

Accurate quantification of anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and their redistribution among Earth’s major carbon reservoirs (atmosphere, oceans, and terrestrial biosphere) is essential for tracking mitigation progress, informing climate policy, and projecting future climate trajectories1–3. As global temperatures rise and the impacts of climate change intensify, the scientific community is refining observational and modeling tools to constrain each component of the carbon cycle. The Paris Agreement’s five-year Global Stocktake further heightens this urgency by requiring transparent, robust assessments of carbon sources and sinks to underpin effective policy-making. Yet persistent, poorly understood variability within the natural carbon cycle still hamper the verification of reported emission reductions under international accords.

Over the past decade, researchers have addressed these shortcomings by acquiring higher-quality observations and activity data, expanding model ensembles, refining parameterizations, and incorporating previously omitted processes—such as cement carbonation and coupled nitrogen–phosphorus dynamics—into land and ocean carbon models4–7. These advances, which we collectively term bottom-up improvements, improve the process models (land and ocean uptake) and inventories (anthropogenic emissions) that underpin contemporary carbon budgets. Although such improvements should, in principle, reduce component-level errors, quantitative evidence of an overall gain in accuracy remains elusive.

CO2 is emitted into the atmosphere due to fossil fuel combustion, industrial processes, and land-use changes. Natural sinks partially offset these emissions with ~25% uptake by oceans and 30% uptake by terrestrial ecosystems, with the remaining 45% accumulating in the atmosphere7. On a global scale, a mass balance exists between annual emissions, sinks, and the CO2 annual growth rate in the atmosphere. The residual imbalance, B I, quantifies our inability to close the budget of fluxes across the Earth’s carbon cycle pools:

B I = E F + E L − S O − S L − S C − G A (1)

All quantities on the equation’s right-hand side denote the component flux estimates in petagram carbon per year (PgC yr−1). E F represents fossil fuel and industrial process emissions, E L denotes land-use change emissions, S O and S L are the oceanic and land uptake, respectively, and S C symbolizes cement carbonation5. G A denotes the atmospheric growth rate of CO2 8, caused by differences between emissions and sinks. The imbalance quantifies the sum of errors in all flux components on the right-hand side, serving as a metric for data imperfections and gaps in our understanding of the contemporary carbon cycle.

Growth rates derived from marine boundary layer (MBL) surface flask (sometimes referred to as in situ measurements) mixing ratio measurements are typically considered highly accurate. Consequently, the budget imbalance has often been attributed primarily to inaccuracies in other components, particularly land and ocean sinks3,7–9. However, the atmospheric growth rate is not directly measured in units of mass change (PgC yr−1) but is derived from mixing ratio measurement changes (ppm yr−1) assuming instantaneous mixing of the fluxes throughout the whole atmosphere. Although surface flask measurements of atmospheric mixing ratios are very accurate and precise, errors are introduced in estimating the whole-atmosphere growth rate due to the sparsity of the MBL surface flask measurement data and methodological assumptions7,10.

Here, we investigate the evolution of collective accuracy using the carbon-budget imbalance reported annually by the Global Carbon Project (GCP). We also quantify the error introduced when the MBL CO2 growth rate is used as a proxy for the whole-atmosphere growth rate. We find that accounting for the discrepancy between MBL and whole-atmosphere growth rates markedly reduces the root-mean-square (RMS) of the annual imbalance time series relative to the values reported in recent GCP Carbon Budget assessments. We further assess the impact of updates to individual budget components between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports, demonstrating that the overall accuracy of Earth’s carbon-budget components has improved over this period.

---

## Results

Whole-atmosphere growth rate correction
The GCP uses growth rate estimates from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Global Monitoring Laboratory, calculated from CO2 mixing ratio observations of well-mixed background air at MBL surface measurement stations. These growth rate estimates serve as the benchmark for most scientific and agency assessments. NOAA estimates the growth rate by smoothing data over time for each MBL station and then averaging it across latitude bands11. GCP converts NOAA growth rate (ppm yr−1) values into the whole-atmosphere mass change (PgC yr−1) using a conversion factor12 of 2.124 PgC ppm−1. This conversion assumes instantaneous mixing—an approximation that introduces errors from finite and varying atmospheric transport timescales and sparse spatiotemporal sampling of MBL observations10. Although the troposphere, which contains about 80% of atmospheric molecules, mixes well within a year, the stratosphere exchanges air slowly with the troposphere over a period ranging from 2–4 years13,14.

Observed stratospheric CO2 mixing ratios are 3–5 ppm lower than tropospheric values, reflecting slow stratosphere–troposphere exchange14,15. Consequently, surface-driven CO2 increases lag in the stratosphere, creating a deficit relative to tropospheric values (see Methods). The GCP acknowledges that using a constant conversion factor of 2.124 PgC ppm−1, an approximation that assumes instantaneous whole-atmosphere mixing, introduces a non-negligible source of uncertainty7. The error introduced by using constant conversion factors to calculate whole-atmosphere growth rates from MBL data can be broken into two errors: troposphere-sampling error and stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) error. The troposphere-sampling error reflects a representativeness error due to the sparsity of MBL sites.

To account for the MBL growth rate discrepancies, we compute the whole-atmosphere CO2 growth rate using two atmospheric flux inversion models: Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS)16 and Jena CarboScope (CS)17. These models optimize emissions and sinks from the oceans and land surfaces to match mixing ratio measurements at surface sites (including many MBL sites) while incorporating STE and additional atmospheric transport and sampling effects through numerical simulations nudged to meteorological reanalysis data (see Methods). Thus, the global integral of the annual net CO2 optimized surface fluxes provides the whole-atmospheric growth rate. Alternatively, to isolate the impact of STE, we employ a simple two-box model representing the troposphere and stratosphere, assuming a 2 year STE timescale (see Methods). This model assumes MBL-derived rates perfectly represent tropospheric growth, isolating only the STE error. The Inverse models (CAMS and Jena CS) account for both troposphere sampling and STE-related errors, while the box model only accounts for the STE-related errors. Note that neither the inversions nor the box models are free of errors. However, we hypothesize that the improvements from accounting for large-scale transport effects like STE and sampling should be more significant, overall leading to a better growth rate estimate and thus reducing the imbalance.

Figure 1 presents various growth rate estimates alongside the corresponding changes in the imbalance reported by GCP in 2023. The long-term mean imbalance does not change after our corrections, but the influence of those corrections is strong during years with pronounced inter-annual variability. This is expected because the STE adjustment acts as a lagged temporal smoother on MBL growth rates when converting them to whole-atmosphere values (see Methods). Because its magnitude depends on the past values of tropospheric mixing ratios, it damps extremes and nudges annual values toward the mean (see Supplementary Section 1).

Two illustrative cases of the impact of growth rate correction are the peak imbalance of +1.7 PgC yr−1 in 1991 and the trough imbalance of −1.5 PgC yr−1 in 1998. These years coincide with the Mount Pinatubo eruption and a strong El Niño, respectively. These events induced sharp perturbations to the carbon cycle and have historically challenged bottom-up models. For 1991, the high imbalance has been linked to an underestimation of the land-sink response, likely due to a lack of representation of diffuse-radiation effects following the volcanic aerosol injection18,19. Our revised growth-rate estimate raises the previously low MBL value in 1991, and lowers the high value in 1998, producing a small but meaningful reduction in both imbalance extremes (CAMS imbalance for 1991 = +1.17 PgC yr−1 and 1998 = −0.87 PgC yr−1). While these years remain prominent anomalies even after the correction, the diminished residual suggests that process models may be more skillful against such climatic shocks than previously assumed.

The annually varying corrections to the growth rate required to account for the STE effect cannot be captured by a single, time-invariant conversion factor. In particular, the widely used 2.124 PgC ppm−1 factor12, derived under the assumptions of a fixed atmospheric mass and uniform, instantaneous mixing, systematically over-estimates high MBL growth years and under-estimates low MBL growth years (see Supplementary Section 1), biasing flux estimates wherever growth rates deviate from the long-term average.

The RMS imbalance in the GCP 2023 report is 0.76 PgC yr−1 for the period of 1985–2016. Applying the box-model-based STE correction reduces the RMS imbalance by 11% (from 0.76 PgC yr−1) to 0.67 PgC yr−1. The atmospheric inversion corrections from Jena CS and CAMS reduce the RMS imbalance by 24% and 25%, leading to imbalances of 0.58 PgC yr−1 for Jena CS and 0.57 PgC yr−1 for CAMS. A stronger improvement from inversions compared to box model is expected because inversions account for additional atmospheric transport dynamics and atmospheric sampling effects.

The whole-atmosphere corrections are significant relative to the budget imbalance, which aggregates the errors of all components. The growth rate correction terms themselves have RMS magnitudes of 0.16, 0.36, and 0.37 PgC yr−1 for the box-model, CAMS, and Jena CS estimates, respectively. For context, the largest of these correction RMS values is 49% of the GCP-2023 RMS imbalance of 0.76 PgC yr−1. These improvements demonstrate that uncertainties in the atmospheric growth rate account for a substantial share of the total imbalance error. The large improvement in the imbalance due to the growth rate corrections also shows that bottom-up models are more accurate than previously perceived, based on the assumption that the imbalance was primarily caused by errors in these bottom-up models.

Improvements in process models and inventories
The GCP carbon budget estimates are updated annually to incorporate data re-evaluation and developments in process understanding, and the use of larger model ensembles7. Consequently, inaccuracies in budget components and the resulting imbalance are expected to decrease over time. We analyze changes in budget components between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports to test this hypothesis. To identify the components causing the imbalance RMS reduction, we calculate an imbalance due to a component change between the 2017 and 2023 reports (see Methods), leaving other components unchanged.

Figure 2 shows the time series of carbon-flux components and the MBL CO2 growth rate from the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports7,8. All components exhibit changes between the 2017 and 2023 estimates, with the largest RMS differences observed in the land-use change (0.23 PgC yr−1), the land sink (0.25 PgC yr−1), and the ocean sink (0.22 PgC yr−1). Fossil-fuel emissions and the MBL growth rate also change notably, with RMS differences of 0.13 PgC yr−1 and 0.07 PgC yr−1, respectively.

A few reasons for the changes in the component estimates are as follows: The GCP ocean sink estimates changed between the 2017 and 2023 reports, with GCP 2023 using a combination of process models and data-driven (fCO2-based20) approaches (as shown in Fig. 2). NOAA MBL flask measurements were recalibrated to the 2019 WMO scale and the derived growth-rate estimates from these recalibrated mixing ratio measurement data were first used in the GCP 2021 report6,21. The growth rates can also change due to stabilization-latency effects in the NOAA MBL time series, which introduce a latency before convergence to the final growth rates levels (see Figure 9 of ref. 10). Beginning with the 2020 GCP report22, the cement-carbonation sink was included after its substantial role in atmospheric CO2 removal was recognized5. Between the 2017 report, in which it was not reported (i.e., assumed zero), and the 2023 report, the RMS difference in this sink is 0.11 PgC yr−1, underscoring its significance.

Figure 3 presents the imbalance RMS change between the two reports. The 16% reduction in the imbalance (from 0.91 to 0.76 PgC yr−1) indicates a significant decrease in the sum of errors. This reduction in imbalance is comparable to the whole-atmospheric growth rate correction when applied to the 2017 GCP report, which results in an RMS imbalance of 0.77 PgC yr−1 when using the CAMS flux inversion (see Supplementary Fig. 1). Note that applying the growth rate correction yields a smaller percentage reduction for the 2017 GCP report (a 15% drop from a 0.91 PgC yr−1 baseline) than for the 2023 GCP report (a 25% drop from a 0.76 PgC yr−1 baseline). This occurs because the total error variance, which mostly determines the RMS of the budget imbalance, is effectively the quadrature sum of variances from multiple error sources (error variances combine in quadrature if independent). Consequently, while a growth rate correction reduces the variance component associated with the growth rate, its fractional impact on the overall RMS is smaller when the initial RMS imbalance (and thus the total underlying error variance) is large due to other substantial uncorrected error components. Therefore, as bottom-up emission and sink estimates continue to improve, growth rate errors will account for an increasingly dominant share of the residual budget imbalance, underscoring the need for further refinement of observational and modeling constraints on global CO2 growth rates.

The colored crosses (and the “+“ signs) in Fig. 3 show the RMS imbalance impact due to different component updates (see Methods). We find that all carbon budget component updates lead to an imbalance reduction. This shows that the component estimates have individually improved, and the imbalance improvement is not due to a compensatory effect where the improvement of one component offsets the worsening of another.

The causes of improving estimates or error reduction can be broken into four broad effects: (1) standard error reduction due to an increase in ensemble size, (2) improvement in process representations, (3) forcing data improvement, and (4) model resolution improvement. The process level improvements stem from numerous individual advancements (see Table 3 of Friedlingstein et al.7, Table S1 of Le Quéré et al.8, and Sitch et al.4). Fossil fuel emission estimates have likely improved due to additional effect of the availability of better emission activity data from emerging economies23.

The carbon budget imbalance analysis presented here can serve as a diagnostic for attributing overall budget improvements to specific component changes. For instance, substituting land sink estimates in the GCP 2023 budget with those from only the six models accounting for diffuse radiation effects yields an RMS imbalance of 0.72 PgC yr−1, a notable reduction from the 0.80 PgC yr−1 obtained using the multi-model mean from the fourteen models omitting this process (all other GCP 2023 components held constant). We also test whether increases in model ensemble sizes are a driver of the observed imbalance reduction between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports, as larger ensembles might theoretically reduce the standard error of the multi-model mean. However, our tests indicate that, for both land and ocean sinks, expanding the ensemble size does not, in itself, lead to a reduction in the budget imbalance. The RMS imbalance for GCP 2023 using only the land sink models present in the 2017 ensemble is 0.758 PgC yr−1, closely aligned with the 0.762 PgC yr−1 RMS imbalance using the full GCP 2023 land model ensemble; a similar outcome is observed for ocean sink estimates. While a complete imbalance attribution of all changes between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports is not undertaken here, the budget imbalance analysis presented here can be utilized in future investigations to quantify the influence of individual modifications.

We also perform a suite of sensitivity tests (see Supplementary Section 2) to check that the declining RMS budget imbalance reported here reflects genuine component estimate improvements. We find consistent imbalance reductions across three independent periods (1960–1984, 1985–2004, and 2005–2016), further corroborating that these advances arise from better forcing data and refined process representations. In Supplementary Section 3, we discuss how the carbon budget imbalance (the net effect of all actual component errors) relates to the GCP-reported uncertainty estimates for these components.

---

## Methods

We analyze the global carbon budget imbalance from 1985 through 2016. The primary baseline budgets are taken from the GCP 20178 and GCP 20237 reports. The analysis starts in 1985. For inversion-based growth rates, this allows for a sufficient spin-up period (e.g., CAMS begins in 1979), accounting for typical stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) timescales of 2–4 years. We estimate the whole-atmosphere growth rate from a box model and as the global, annual integral of the net surface CO2 fluxes optimized by the CAMS and Jena CS atmospheric inversion systems. The whole-atmosphere growth rate is theoretically equal to the net fluxes, which are mainly due to surface emissions and sinks, except for a minor contribution from CO oxidation.

Atmospheric inversions
CAMS. The CO2 atmospheric inversion of the operational Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) assimilates atmospheric mixing ratio observations (surface air-sample measurements) in the LMDz atmospheric transport model. During the assimilation process, the LMDz model is inverted in a variational framework to yield statistically optimal CO2 surface emissions and sinks at weekly and grid-point scales. For CAMS version v22r1 used here, available surface air-sample measurements at 159 sites between January 1979 and March 2023 were assimilated; the model resolution was 79 layers in the vertical, 1.27° in latitude and 2.5° in longitude. More details on the inversion system can be found in Chevallier et al.16, and references therein.

Jena CarboScope (CS). Atmospheric tracer transport in the Jena CarboScope inversions is simulated by the TM3 atmospheric chemical transport model at a resolution of ~4° in latitude by 5° in longitude, with 19 vertical layers driven by meteorological fields from the NCEP (National Centers for Environmental Prediction) reanalysis. The run “s76_v2023” of the Jena CarboScope employed here uses 8 atmospheric CO2 measurement sites that span its estimation period from 1976 to 2022. CarboScope uses a fossil-fuel CO2 emission prior from GridFED, an ocean CO2 exchange prior based on the interpolation of SOCAT pCO2 data. In contrast to the CarboScope run used in the GCP 2023 report, the run s76_v2023 used here has explicit interannual degrees of freedom (i.e., no regression against predictor variables). For more details on the setup, see Appendix A of17, with slight updates described on the website of CarboScope24.

Although the two inversions differ in aspects such as the number of assimilated measurement-site networks and vertical model resolution, they both incorporate data from a common core MBL network. This MBL network provides the primary observational constraint for estimating the annual global CO2 growth rate in these inversions. Both inversions are designed to track the global CO2 growth rate while also capturing key transport processes, including stratosphere-troposphere exchange.

To demonstrate that the inversions not only reproduce the MBL observations but also capture large-scale transport effects—such as the slow stratosphere–troposphere exchange—we compare the CAMS-inversion–simulated CO2 mole fractions against NOAA MBL observations (Supplementary Fig. 2)25 and AirCore profiles (Supplementary Fig. 3)26. Our analysis shows that the optimized CAMS fields reproduce the MBL mixing ratio measurements and resolve the stratosphere–troposphere CO2 mixing ratio gradient observed by AirCore.

Two-box model
To isolate the impact of stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) on the inferred whole-atmosphere CO2 growth rate, we employ a two-box model representing the troposphere and stratosphere. This model simulates the exchange of CO2 between these two reservoirs, where air is exchanged carrying the CO2 mixing ratio of its box of origin. The net rate of CO2 mixing ratio change in each box is driven by the difference in their respective CO2 mixing ratios, modulated by a characteristic exchange timescale.

Let C tropo(t) and C strato(t) denote the mean CO2 mixing ratios (in ppm) in the troposphere and stratosphere, respectively, at time t. We use K atm = 2.124 PgC ppm−1 as the conversion factor representing the CO2 mass required to raise the mean atmospheric mixing ratio by 1 ppm12. The troposphere is assumed to contain a fraction f tropo = 0.8 of the total atmospheric air mass, and the stratosphere a fraction f strato = 0.213.

The model dynamics are described by the following system of ordinary differential equations:

dC strato(t) / dt = (C tropo(t) − C strato(t)) / τ (2)

dC tropo(t) / dt = (E net(t) / (f tropo * K atm)) − (f strato * (C tropo(t) − C strato(t)) / (f tropo * τ)) (3)

Here, τ is the characteristic exchange timescale between the two boxes, representing the e-folding time for stratospheric mixing ratio adjustment (i.e., the stratospheric air residence time). E net(t) (in PgC yr−1) denotes the net CO2 flux (from surface sources/sinks and atmospheric chemical production) entering the troposphere. The factor f strato / f tropo in Eq. 3 ensures CO2 mass conservation during exchange between the reservoirs with differing air masses.

Our objective is to estimate E net(t), which serves as the box-model derived whole-atmosphere CO2 growth rate (G box A), based on observed tropospheric CO2 changes. Rearranging Eq. 3 yields:

E net(t) = f tropo * K atm * [dC tropo(t) / dt + (f strato / f tropo) * (C tropo(t) − C strato(t)) / τ] (4)

We first estimate the time series of tropospheric CO2 mixing ratio C tropo(t) using the annual CO2 growth rates from the GCP 2023 report as dC tropo(t) / dt and the initial condition C tropo(0) = 280 ppm in the year 1750 (t=0). The stratospheric CO2 mixing ratio can also be expressed analytically as:

C strato(t) = e−t/τ * C strato(0) + (1/τ) * ∫ (from 0 to t) C tropo(s) ds (5)

C strato(t) is then obtained by numerically integrating Eq. 5 initialized with C strato(0) = 280 ppm. This formulation shows that C strato(t) depends on its initial state and past tropospheric mixing ratios. It is an exponentially weighted moving average of tropospheric mixing ratios with characteristic timescale τ. This “stratospheric memory” effect imposes a lagged temporal smoothing when inferring whole-atmosphere growth rate from tropospheric CO2 changes. With C tropo(t), its derivative dC tropo(t) / dt, and the calculated C strato(t) (using scipy.integrate module in Python for Eq. 5), we compute E net(t) using Eq. 4.

A STE time τ of 2 years was implemented in the box model. The simulated CO2 mixing ratios and the resulting stratosphere-troposphere mixing ratio difference from this box model are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4. This simulated difference aligns well with observed differences from AirCore profiles and CAMS 3D mole fraction field data. Sensitivity tests assessing the influence of varying τ on the budget imbalance reduction are presented in Supplementary Table 1.

Individual component’s imbalance impact
To isolate the impact of updates to an individual carbon budget component C on the overall budget imbalance, we recalculate the imbalance time series by starting with the budget imbalance from the 2017 GCP report (B IM,17) and effectively substitute the 2017 estimate of component C (C 17) with its 2023 estimate (C 23), while keeping all other components at their 2017 values.

The resulting imbalance due to the update in the component C, denoted B IM,C, is calculated as:

B IM,C = B IM,17 + δ C * (C 23 − C 17) (6)

Here, C 17 and C 23 are the multi-model mean estimates for component C from the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports, respectively. The factor δ C is +1 if component C is a source term in Eq. 1 (i.e., fossil emissions E F or land-use change emissions E L). Conversely, δ C is −1 if component C is a sink term (ocean sink S O, land sink S L, cement carbonation S C) or the atmospheric growth rate (G A), assuming these sink/growth values are positive numbers in the component data. The term (C 23 − C 17) represents the change in the estimate of component C between the two reports.

Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need for more evidence that our
whole-atmosphere CO₂ growth rate (AGR) estimates are more accurate than the
marine boundary layer (MBL) series. Below, we clarify why the revised growth rate
estimates are better founded physically and empirically, and why their use is preferable
to inflating the MBL growth rate uncertainty.
The CO₂ measurement and modelling community is aware that stratospheric-
tropospheric mixing is an issue. Early observations of stratospheric CO₂ by Georgii et
al. (1969) using aircraft showed a 3-5 ppm drop in CO₂ concentrations. They noted,
“The marked decrease of the CO₂ concentration in the lower stratosphere compared
with the upper troposphere suggests that, contrary to previous practice, it is wrong to
assume a constant mixing-ratio of CO₂ in the troposphere and stratosphere.” Global
Carbon Project (GCP 2023 report) reports also note that, “The fourth factor is the
uncertainty associated with using the average CO₂ concentration from a surface
network to approximate the true atmospheric average CO₂ concentration (mass-
weighted, in three dimensions) as needed to assess the total atmospheric CO₂ burden.
In reality, CO₂ variations measured at the stations will not exactly track changes in total
atmospheric burden, with offsets in magnitude and phasing due to vertical and
horizontal mixing.”
So, the use of instantaneous whole-atmosphere mixing assumption introduces errors.
However, it has been assumed that this error is minor relative to the errors in the rest of
the carbon budget components. Nevertheless, a quantitative test of these errors against
the errors in other components has never been performed. Recently, Pandey et al. 2024
investigated the whole-atmosphere growth rate errors resulting from using MBL sites
and found the error to be 0.25 PgC per year (or 0.12 ppm per year) for the period 2015-
2019. This error includes stratosphere-troposphere exchange errors as well as within-
troposphere sampling errors.
An atmospheric inversion system produces the whole-atmosphere growth rate, which is
exactly equal to the sum of the fluxes added over a year. Inversion systems assimilate
the observations used to calculate the NOAA MBL growth rate. However, they also
represent 3D atmospheric transport using meteorological data. CAMS, for example,
assimilates the same NOAA flask data used to produce the NOAA MBL observations,
but it also accounts for vertical transport. The vertical gradients of these models are
validated using aircraft and satellite retrievals, explicitly resolve 3-D transport, and
include STE.
To address the reviewer’s concern, we validated the simulated model‑fraction field from
the CAMS inversion against in situ observations. Using the NOAA Marine Boundary
Layer Observation Network sites, CAMS reproduces the MBL CO₂ measurements with
high fidelity (SI Figure 7). This agreement demonstrates that CAMS not only employs
the same observational constraints as the NOAA MBL calculation but also accurately
matches them. As a full atmospheric inversion, CAMS also accounts for transport
processes such as stratosphere–troposphere exchange. To assess this, we compared
CAMS‑simulated CO₂ mixing‑ratio fields with independent AirCore observations. In
2016, observed stratospheric air-core profiles are 4-5 ppm lower than the tropospheric
average, and CAMS successfully captures this reduction (SI Figure 6) while also
matching the NOAA MBL observations well. In summary, CAMS captures the MBL CO2
growth rate and STE transport, and the integration of surface carbon fluxes over a year
from CAMS represents the carbon released to the whole atmosphere, thus, the
atmospheric CO2 growth rate based on CAMS is more accurate.
The box-model solution presented here is a simple parametric correction that accounts
only for stratosphere–troposphere exchange time. Its primary objective is to simulate
the CO₂ mixing ratio difference induced by this exchange. We provide an analytical
solution that can be readily applied to NOAA MBL growth rates, yielding a substantial
AGR correction and a corresponding reduction in the global carbon-budget imbalance.
The box model assumes an exchange time of 2 years, based on 80% of the
atmospheric mass residing in the troposphere. To validate this exchange time, we
compared the simulated stratosphere–troposphere CO₂ mixing ratio difference with
AirCore observations and CAMS-simulated 3D mole fraction fields. We extracted the
CAMS 3D mole fraction fields for 2016 and computed the annual mean CO₂ gradient
across the 200 hPa boundary (SI Figure 5). We found a stratosphere–troposphere CO₂
mixing ratio difference of 4–5 ppm in 2016, which is consistent with both CAMS and the
AirCore observations, confirming that our chosen exchange timescale for the 200 hPa
box is a reasonable estimate. Note that the CAMS mole-fraction fields have already
been validated against NOAA MBL as well as independent aircraft and air-core profiles.
Overall, the whole-atmospheric conversion error arises from well-understood physical
effects, the main one being the finite rate of STE. Because the STE bias arises from a
well-understood physical process that can be parameterized (box model) or explicitly
simulated (inverse models), we argue that these errors that can be corrected for using
established models.

Response: We agree with the reviewer that we expect the models to improve over time.
Our study seeks to move beyond this general intuition. Specifically, our objective is to
quantify the magnitude of these advancements and, to delineate the specific
components responsible for driving them. We believe our detailed investigation offers
distinct contributions:
1. Firstly, we introduce a quantitative benchmark for evaluating community-wide
progress. Through a comparative analysis of successive Global Carbon Project
(GCP) releases, we demonstrate a notable 16% reduction in the 1985–2016
RMS budget imbalance (from 0.91 to 0.76 Pg C yr⁻¹). To the best of our
knowledge, this constitutes the first objective, end-to-end metric for assessing
progress within the global carbon-budget modeling community.
2. Secondly, our research provides a component-level attribution of this observed
net gain. By propagating each updated term through our analytical framework,
we reveal that the improvements are not localized to a single component.
Instead, they are distributed across multiple elements, including the ocean sink,
land sink, land-use change emissions, atmospheric growth rate, and fossil-fuel
emissions.
3. Thirdly, in response to comments from Reviewer #3, we conducted an additional
experiment designed to determine whether the documented gains are
attributable to enhanced process realism or are merely statistical artifacts. Our
findings, derived from substituting the full ensemble of 20 DGVMs with a targeted
subset of six models that explicitly incorporate diffuse radiation effects, show a
further reduction in the RMS imbalance to 0.72 Pg C yr⁻¹. Conversely, a simple
expansion of the DGVM ensemble size from 15 to 20 models yielded no
discernible improvement. This suggests that the accurate representation of key
physical processes is a more critical determinant of model advancement than
sheer ensemble size.

## Paper

## Abstract

The Global Carbon Project (GCP) compiles an updated global carbon budget each year, synthesizing state-of-the-art estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions, land and ocean sinks, and the atmospheric CO2 growth rate. The residual between these terms, referred to as the global carbon budget imbalance, reflects the aggregate inaccuracies of the individual component estimates. Growth rates derived from marine boundary layer (MBL) surface flask mixing ratio observations are assumed to be highly accurate. Hence, land and ocean sink estimates from process models are viewed as the primary source of the imbalance. Here we show that substantial discrepancies arise when marine boundary layer growth rate estimates are used to represent the whole atmosphere. Correcting for this discrepancy using atmospheric flux inversion estimates reduces the 0.76 petagrams of carbon per year (PgC yr−1) root-mean-square (RMS) imbalance (from the 2023 GCP report) by up to 25%. Further investigation into the imbalance metric between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports shows a reduction in imbalance resulting from updates to each carbon budget component, leading to a 16% overall reduction. These reductions provide quantitative evidence of improvements in process models and inventory emission estimates, driven by enhanced forcing data and the inclusion of new carbon cycle processes. Overall, we report a 37% reduction in the root-mean-square imbalance, from 0.91 to 0.57 PgC yr−1, between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports by combining process model and inventory improvements with atmospheric growth rate corrections. Our findings indicate that land and ocean process models are more accurate than previously believed and that the scientific understanding of Earth’s carbon cycle is improving.

---

## Introduction

Accurate quantification of anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and their redistribution among Earth’s major carbon reservoirs (atmosphere, oceans, and terrestrial biosphere) is essential for tracking mitigation progress, informing climate policy, and projecting future climate trajectories1–3. As global temperatures rise and the impacts of climate change intensify, the scientific community is refining observational and modeling tools to constrain each component of the carbon cycle. The Paris Agreement’s five-year Global Stocktake further heightens this urgency by requiring transparent, robust assessments of carbon sources and sinks to underpin effective policy-making. Yet persistent, poorly understood variability within the natural carbon cycle still hamper the verification of reported emission reductions under international accords.

Over the past decade, researchers have addressed these shortcomings by acquiring higher-quality observations and activity data, expanding model ensembles, refining parameterizations, and incorporating previously omitted processes—such as cement carbonation and coupled nitrogen–phosphorus dynamics—into land and ocean carbon models4–7. These advances, which we collectively term bottom-up improvements, improve the process models (land and ocean uptake) and inventories (anthropogenic emissions) that underpin contemporary carbon budgets. Although such improvements should, in principle, reduce component-level errors, quantitative evidence of an overall gain in accuracy remains elusive.

CO2 is emitted into the atmosphere due to fossil fuel combustion, industrial processes, and land-use changes. Natural sinks partially offset these emissions with ~25% uptake by oceans and 30% uptake by terrestrial ecosystems, with the remaining 45% accumulating in the atmosphere7. On a global scale, a mass balance exists between annual emissions, sinks, and the CO2 annual growth rate in the atmosphere. The residual imbalance, B I, quantifies our inability to close the budget of fluxes across the Earth’s carbon cycle pools:

B I = E F + E L − S O − S L − S C − G A (1)

All quantities on the equation’s right-hand side denote the component flux estimates in petagram carbon per year (PgC yr−1). E F represents fossil fuel and industrial process emissions, E L denotes land-use change emissions, S O and S L are the oceanic and land uptake, respectively, and S C symbolizes cement carbonation5. G A denotes the atmospheric growth rate of CO2 8, caused by differences between emissions and sinks. The imbalance quantifies the sum of errors in all flux components on the right-hand side, serving as a metric for data imperfections and gaps in our understanding of the contemporary carbon cycle.

Growth rates derived from marine boundary layer (MBL) surface flask (sometimes referred to as in situ measurements) mixing ratio measurements are typically considered highly accurate. Consequently, the budget imbalance has often been attributed primarily to inaccuracies in other components, particularly land and ocean sinks3,7–9. However, the atmospheric growth rate is not directly measured in units of mass change (PgC yr−1) but is derived from mixing ratio measurement changes (ppm yr−1) assuming instantaneous mixing of the fluxes throughout the whole atmosphere. Although surface flask measurements of atmospheric mixing ratios are very accurate and precise, errors are introduced in estimating the whole-atmosphere growth rate due to the sparsity of the MBL surface flask measurement data and methodological assumptions7,10.

Here, we investigate the evolution of collective accuracy using the carbon-budget imbalance reported annually by the Global Carbon Project (GCP). We also quantify the error introduced when the MBL CO2 growth rate is used as a proxy for the whole-atmosphere growth rate. We find that accounting for the discrepancy between MBL and whole-atmosphere growth rates markedly reduces the root-mean-square (RMS) of the annual imbalance time series relative to the values reported in recent GCP Carbon Budget assessments. We further assess the impact of updates to individual budget components between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports, demonstrating that the overall accuracy of Earth’s carbon-budget components has improved over this period.

## Results

Whole-atmosphere growth rate correction
The GCP uses growth rate estimates from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Global Monitoring Laboratory, calculated from CO2 mixing ratio observations of well-mixed background air at MBL surface measurement stations. These growth rate estimates serve as the benchmark for most scientific and agency assessments. NOAA estimates the growth rate by smoothing data over time for each MBL station and then averaging it across latitude bands11. GCP converts NOAA growth rate (ppm yr−1) values into the whole-atmosphere mass change (PgC yr−1) using a conversion factor12 of 2.124 PgC ppm−1. This conversion assumes instantaneous mixing—an approximation that introduces errors from finite and varying atmospheric transport timescales and sparse spatiotemporal sampling of MBL observations10. Although the troposphere, which contains about 80% of atmospheric molecules, mixes well within a year, the stratosphere exchanges air slowly with the troposphere over a period ranging from 2–4 years13,14.

Observed stratospheric CO2 mixing ratios are 3–5 ppm lower than tropospheric values, reflecting slow stratosphere–troposphere exchange14,15. Consequently, surface-driven CO2 increases lag in the stratosphere, creating a deficit relative to tropospheric values (see Methods). The GCP acknowledges that using a constant conversion factor of 2.124 PgC ppm−1, an approximation that assumes instantaneous whole-atmosphere mixing, introduces a non-negligible source of uncertainty7. The error introduced by using constant conversion factors to calculate whole-atmosphere growth rates from MBL data can be broken into two errors: troposphere-sampling error and stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) error. The troposphere-sampling error reflects a representativeness error due to the sparsity of MBL sites.

To account for the MBL growth rate discrepancies, we compute the whole-atmosphere CO2 growth rate using two atmospheric flux inversion models: Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS)16 and Jena CarboScope (CS)17. These models optimize emissions and sinks from the oceans and land surfaces to match mixing ratio measurements at surface sites (including many MBL sites) while incorporating STE and additional atmospheric transport and sampling effects through numerical simulations nudged to meteorological reanalysis data (see Methods). Thus, the global integral of the annual net CO2 optimized surface fluxes provides the whole-atmospheric growth rate. Alternatively, to isolate the impact of STE, we employ a simple two-box model representing the troposphere and stratosphere, assuming a 2 year STE timescale (see Methods). This model assumes MBL-derived rates perfectly represent tropospheric growth, isolating only the STE error. The Inverse models (CAMS and Jena CS) account for both troposphere sampling and STE-related errors, while the box model only accounts for the STE-related errors. Note that neither the inversions nor the box models are free of errors. However, we hypothesize that the improvements from accounting for large-scale transport effects like STE and sampling should be more significant, overall leading to a better growth rate estimate and thus reducing the imbalance.

Figure 1 presents various growth rate estimates alongside the corresponding changes in the imbalance reported by GCP in 2023. The long-term mean imbalance does not change after our corrections, but the influence of those corrections is strong during years with pronounced inter-annual variability. This is expected because the STE adjustment acts as a lagged temporal smoother on MBL growth rates when converting them to whole-atmosphere values (see Methods). Because its magnitude depends on the past values of tropospheric mixing ratios, it damps extremes and nudges annual values toward the mean (see Supplementary Section 1).

Two illustrative cases of the impact of growth rate correction are the peak imbalance of +1.7 PgC yr−1 in 1991 and the trough imbalance of −1.5 PgC yr−1 in 1998. These years coincide with the Mount Pinatubo eruption and a strong El Niño, respectively. These events induced sharp perturbations to the carbon cycle and have historically challenged bottom-up models. For 1991, the high imbalance has been linked to an underestimation of the land-sink response, likely due to a lack of representation of diffuse-radiation effects following the volcanic aerosol injection18,19. Our revised growth-rate estimate raises the previously low MBL value in 1991, and lowers the high value in 1998, producing a small but meaningful reduction in both imbalance extremes (CAMS imbalance for 1991 = +1.17 PgC yr−1 and 1998 = −0.87 PgC yr−1). While these years remain prominent anomalies even after the correction, the diminished residual suggests that process models may be more skillful against such climatic shocks than previously assumed.

The annually varying corrections to the growth rate required to account for the STE effect cannot be captured by a single, time-invariant conversion factor. In particular, the widely used 2.124 PgC ppm−1 factor12, derived under the assumptions of a fixed atmospheric mass and uniform, instantaneous mixing, systematically over-estimates high MBL growth years and under-estimates low MBL growth years (see Supplementary Section 1), biasing flux estimates wherever growth rates deviate from the long-term average.

The RMS imbalance in the GCP 2023 report is 0.76 PgC yr−1 for the period of 1985–2016. Applying the box-model-based STE correction reduces the RMS imbalance by 11% (from 0.76 PgC yr−1) to 0.67 PgC yr−1. The atmospheric inversion corrections from Jena CS and CAMS reduce the RMS imbalance by 24% and 25%, leading to imbalances of 0.58 PgC yr−1 for Jena CS and 0.57 PgC yr−1 for CAMS. A stronger improvement from inversions compared to box model is expected because inversions account for additional atmospheric transport dynamics and atmospheric sampling effects.

The whole-atmosphere corrections are significant relative to the budget imbalance, which aggregates the errors of all components. The growth rate correction terms themselves have RMS magnitudes of 0.16, 0.36, and 0.37 PgC yr−1 for the box-model, CAMS, and Jena CS estimates, respectively. For context, the largest of these correction RMS values is 49% of the GCP-2023 RMS imbalance of 0.76 PgC yr−1. These improvements demonstrate that uncertainties in the atmospheric growth rate account for a substantial share of the total imbalance error. The large improvement in the imbalance due to the growth rate corrections also shows that bottom-up models are more accurate than previously perceived, based on the assumption that the imbalance was primarily caused by errors in these bottom-up models.

Improvements in process models and inventories
The GCP carbon budget estimates are updated annually to incorporate data re-evaluation and developments in process understanding, and the use of larger model ensembles7. Consequently, inaccuracies in budget components and the resulting imbalance are expected to decrease over time. We analyze changes in budget components between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports to test this hypothesis. To identify the components causing the imbalance RMS reduction, we calculate an imbalance due to a component change between the 2017 and 2023 reports (see Methods), leaving other components unchanged.

Figure 2 shows the time series of carbon-flux components and the MBL CO2 growth rate from the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports7,8. All components exhibit changes between the 2017 and 2023 estimates, with the largest RMS differences observed in the land-use change (0.23 PgC yr−1), the land sink (0.25 PgC yr−1), and the ocean sink (0.22 PgC yr−1). Fossil-fuel emissions and the MBL growth rate also change notably, with RMS differences of 0.13 PgC yr−1 and 0.07 PgC yr−1, respectively.

A few reasons for the changes in the component estimates are as follows: The GCP ocean sink estimates changed between the 2017 and 2023 reports, with GCP 2023 using a combination of process models and data-driven (fCO2-based20) approaches (as shown in Fig. 2). NOAA MBL flask measurements were recalibrated to the 2019 WMO scale and the derived growth-rate estimates from these recalibrated mixing ratio measurement data were first used in the GCP 2021 report6,21. The growth rates can also change due to stabilization-latency effects in the NOAA MBL time series, which introduce a latency before convergence to the final growth rates levels (see Figure 9 of ref. 10). Beginning with the 2020 GCP report22, the cement-carbonation sink was included after its substantial role in atmospheric CO2 removal was recognized5. Between the 2017 report, in which it was not reported (i.e., assumed zero), and the 2023 report, the RMS difference in this sink is 0.11 PgC yr−1, underscoring its significance.

Figure 3 presents the imbalance RMS change between the two reports. The 16% reduction in the imbalance (from 0.91 to 0.76 PgC yr−1) indicates a significant decrease in the sum of errors. This reduction in imbalance is comparable to the whole-atmospheric growth rate correction when applied to the 2017 GCP report, which results in an RMS imbalance of 0.77 PgC yr−1 when using the CAMS flux inversion (see Supplementary Fig. 1). Note that applying the growth rate correction yields a smaller percentage reduction for the 2017 GCP report (a 15% drop from a 0.91 PgC yr−1 baseline) than for the 2023 GCP report (a 25% drop from a 0.76 PgC yr−1 baseline). This occurs because the total error variance, which mostly determines the RMS of the budget imbalance, is effectively the quadrature sum of variances from multiple error sources (error variances combine in quadrature if independent). Consequently, while a growth rate correction reduces the variance component associated with the growth rate, its fractional impact on the overall RMS is smaller when the initial RMS imbalance (and thus the total underlying error variance) is large due to other substantial uncorrected error components. Therefore, as bottom-up emission and sink estimates continue to improve, growth rate errors will account for an increasingly dominant share of the residual budget imbalance, underscoring the need for further refinement of observational and modeling constraints on global CO2 growth rates.

The colored crosses (and the “+“ signs) in Fig. 3 show the RMS imbalance impact due to different component updates (see Methods). We find that all carbon budget component updates lead to an imbalance reduction. This shows that the component estimates have individually improved, and the imbalance improvement is not due to a compensatory effect where the improvement of one component offsets the worsening of another.

The causes of improving estimates or error reduction can be broken into four broad effects: (1) standard error reduction due to an increase in ensemble size, (2) improvement in process representations, (3) forcing data improvement, and (4) model resolution improvement. The process level improvements stem from numerous individual advancements (see Table 3 of Friedlingstein et al.7, Table S1 of Le Quéré et al.8, and Sitch et al.4). Fossil fuel emission estimates have likely improved due to additional effect of the availability of better emission activity data from emerging economies23.

The carbon budget imbalance analysis presented here can serve as a diagnostic for attributing overall budget improvements to specific component changes. For instance, substituting land sink estimates in the GCP 2023 budget with those from only the six models accounting for diffuse radiation effects yields an RMS imbalance of 0.72 PgC yr−1, a notable reduction from the 0.80 PgC yr−1 obtained using the multi-model mean from the fourteen models omitting this process (all other GCP 2023 components held constant). We also test whether increases in model ensemble sizes are a driver of the observed imbalance reduction between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports, as larger ensembles might theoretically reduce the standard error of the multi-model mean. However, our tests indicate that, for both land and ocean sinks, expanding the ensemble size does not, in itself, lead to a reduction in the budget imbalance. The RMS imbalance for GCP 2023 using only the land sink models present in the 2017 ensemble is 0.758 PgC yr−1, closely aligned with the 0.762 PgC yr−1 RMS imbalance using the full GCP 2023 land model ensemble; a similar outcome is observed for ocean sink estimates. While a complete imbalance attribution of all changes between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports is not undertaken here, the budget imbalance analysis presented here can be utilized in future investigations to quantify the influence of individual modifications.

We also perform a suite of sensitivity tests (see Supplementary Section 2) to check that the declining RMS budget imbalance reported here reflects genuine component estimate improvements. We find consistent imbalance reductions across three independent periods (1960–1984, 1985–2004, and 2005–2016), further corroborating that these advances arise from better forcing data and refined process representations. In Supplementary Section 3, we discuss how the carbon budget imbalance (the net effect of all actual component errors) relates to the GCP-reported uncertainty estimates for these components.

## Methods

We analyze the global carbon budget imbalance from 1985 through 2016. The primary baseline budgets are taken from the GCP 20178 and GCP 20237 reports. The analysis starts in 1985. For inversion-based growth rates, this allows for a sufficient spin-up period (e.g., CAMS begins in 1979), accounting for typical stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) timescales of 2–4 years. We estimate the whole-atmosphere growth rate from a box model and as the global, annual integral of the net surface CO2 fluxes optimized by the CAMS and Jena CS atmospheric inversion systems. The whole-atmosphere growth rate is theoretically equal to the net fluxes, which are mainly due to surface emissions and sinks, except for a minor contribution from CO oxidation.

Atmospheric inversions
CAMS. The CO2 atmospheric inversion of the operational Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) assimilates atmospheric mixing ratio observations (surface air-sample measurements) in the LMDz atmospheric transport model. During the assimilation process, the LMDz model is inverted in a variational framework to yield statistically optimal CO2 surface emissions and sinks at weekly and grid-point scales. For CAMS version v22r1 used here, available surface air-sample measurements at 159 sites between January 1979 and March 2023 were assimilated; the model resolution was 79 layers in the vertical, 1.27° in latitude and 2.5° in longitude. More details on the inversion system can be found in Chevallier et al.16, and references therein.

Jena CarboScope (CS). Atmospheric tracer transport in the Jena CarboScope inversions is simulated by the TM3 atmospheric chemical transport model at a resolution of ~4° in latitude by 5° in longitude, with 19 vertical layers driven by meteorological fields from the NCEP (National Centers for Environmental Prediction) reanalysis. The run “s76_v2023” of the Jena CarboScope employed here uses 8 atmospheric CO2 measurement sites that span its estimation period from 1976 to 2022. CarboScope uses a fossil-fuel CO2 emission prior from GridFED, an ocean CO2 exchange prior based on the interpolation of SOCAT pCO2 data. In contrast to the CarboScope run used in the GCP 2023 report, the run s76_v2023 used here has explicit interannual degrees of freedom (i.e., no regression against predictor variables). For more details on the setup, see Appendix A of17, with slight updates described on the website of CarboScope24.

Although the two inversions differ in aspects such as the number of assimilated measurement-site networks and vertical model resolution, they both incorporate data from a common core MBL network. This MBL network provides the primary observational constraint for estimating the annual global CO2 growth rate in these inversions. Both inversions are designed to track the global CO2 growth rate while also capturing key transport processes, including stratosphere-troposphere exchange.

To demonstrate that the inversions not only reproduce the MBL observations but also capture large-scale transport effects—such as the slow stratosphere–troposphere exchange—we compare the CAMS-inversion–simulated CO2 mole fractions against NOAA MBL observations (Supplementary Fig. 2)25 and AirCore profiles (Supplementary Fig. 3)26. Our analysis shows that the optimized CAMS fields reproduce the MBL mixing ratio measurements and resolve the stratosphere–troposphere CO2 mixing ratio gradient observed by AirCore.

Two-box model
To isolate the impact of stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) on the inferred whole-atmosphere CO2 growth rate, we employ a two-box model representing the troposphere and stratosphere. This model simulates the exchange of CO2 between these two reservoirs, where air is exchanged carrying the CO2 mixing ratio of its box of origin. The net rate of CO2 mixing ratio change in each box is driven by the difference in their respective CO2 mixing ratios, modulated by a characteristic exchange timescale.

Let C tropo(t) and C strato(t) denote the mean CO2 mixing ratios (in ppm) in the troposphere and stratosphere, respectively, at time t. We use K atm = 2.124 PgC ppm−1 as the conversion factor representing the CO2 mass required to raise the mean atmospheric mixing ratio by 1 ppm12. The troposphere is assumed to contain a fraction f tropo = 0.8 of the total atmospheric air mass, and the stratosphere a fraction f strato = 0.213.

The model dynamics are described by the following system of ordinary differential equations:

dC strato(t) / dt = (C tropo(t) − C strato(t)) / τ (2)

dC tropo(t) / dt = (E net(t) / (f tropo * K atm)) − (f strato * (C tropo(t) − C strato(t)) / (f tropo * τ)) (3)

Here, τ is the characteristic exchange timescale between the two boxes, representing the e-folding time for stratospheric mixing ratio adjustment (i.e., the stratospheric air residence time). E net(t) (in PgC yr−1) denotes the net CO2 flux (from surface sources/sinks and atmospheric chemical production) entering the troposphere. The factor f strato / f tropo in Eq. 3 ensures CO2 mass conservation during exchange between the reservoirs with differing air masses.

Our objective is to estimate E net(t), which serves as the box-model derived whole-atmosphere CO2 growth rate (G box A), based on observed tropospheric CO2 changes. Rearranging Eq. 3 yields:

E net(t) = f tropo * K atm * [dC tropo(t) / dt + (f strato / f tropo) * (C tropo(t) − C strato(t)) / τ] (4)

We first estimate the time series of tropospheric CO2 mixing ratio C tropo(t) using the annual CO2 growth rates from the GCP 2023 report as dC tropo(t) / dt and the initial condition C tropo(0) = 280 ppm in the year 1750 (t=0). The stratospheric CO2 mixing ratio can also be expressed analytically as:

C strato(t) = e−t/τ * C strato(0) + (1/τ) * ∫ (from 0 to t) C tropo(s) ds (5)

C strato(t) is then obtained by numerically integrating Eq. 5 initialized with C strato(0) = 280 ppm. This formulation shows that C strato(t) depends on its initial state and past tropospheric mixing ratios. It is an exponentially weighted moving average of tropospheric mixing ratios with characteristic timescale τ. This “stratospheric memory” effect imposes a lagged temporal smoothing when inferring whole-atmosphere growth rate from tropospheric CO2 changes. With C tropo(t), its derivative dC tropo(t) / dt, and the calculated C strato(t) (using scipy.integrate module in Python for Eq. 5), we compute E net(t) using Eq. 4.

A STE time τ of 2 years was implemented in the box model. The simulated CO2 mixing ratios and the resulting stratosphere-troposphere mixing ratio difference from this box model are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4. This simulated difference aligns well with observed differences from AirCore profiles and CAMS 3D mole fraction field data. Sensitivity tests assessing the influence of varying τ on the budget imbalance reduction are presented in Supplementary Table 1.

Individual component’s imbalance impact
To isolate the impact of updates to an individual carbon budget component C on the overall budget imbalance, we recalculate the imbalance time series by starting with the budget imbalance from the 2017 GCP report (B IM,17) and effectively substitute the 2017 estimate of component C (C 17) with its 2023 estimate (C 23), while keeping all other components at their 2017 values.

The resulting imbalance due to the update in the component C, denoted B IM,C, is calculated as:

B IM,C = B IM,17 + δ C * (C 23 − C 17) (6)

Here, C 17 and C 23 are the multi-model mean estimates for component C from the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports, respectively. The factor δ C is +1 if component C is a source term in Eq. 1 (i.e., fossil emissions E F or land-use change emissions E L). Conversely, δ C is −1 if component C is a sink term (ocean sink S O, land sink S L, cement carbonation S C) or the atmospheric growth rate (G A), assuming these sink/growth values are positive numbers in the component data. The term (C 23 − C 17) represents the change in the estimate of component C between the two reports.

Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need for more evidence that our
whole-atmosphere CO₂ growth rate (AGR) estimates are more accurate than the
marine boundary layer (MBL) series. Below, we clarify why the revised growth rate
estimates are better founded physically and empirically, and why their use is preferable
to inflating the MBL growth rate uncertainty.
The CO₂ measurement and modelling community is aware that stratospheric-
tropospheric mixing is an issue. Early observations of stratospheric CO₂ by Georgii et
al. (1969) using aircraft showed a 3-5 ppm drop in CO₂ concentrations. They noted,
“The marked decrease of the CO₂ concentration in the lower stratosphere compared
with the upper troposphere suggests that, contrary to previous practice, it is wrong to
assume a constant mixing-ratio of CO₂ in the troposphere and stratosphere.” Global
Carbon Project (GCP 2023 report) reports also note that, “The fourth factor is the
uncertainty associated with using the average CO₂ concentration from a surface
network to approximate the true atmospheric average CO₂ concentration (mass-
weighted, in three dimensions) as needed to assess the total atmospheric CO₂ burden.
In reality, CO₂ variations measured at the stations will not exactly track changes in total
atmospheric burden, with offsets in magnitude and phasing due to vertical and
horizontal mixing.”
So, the use of instantaneous whole-atmosphere mixing assumption introduces errors.
However, it has been assumed that this error is minor relative to the errors in the rest of
the carbon budget components. Nevertheless, a quantitative test of these errors against
the errors in other components has never been performed. Recently, Pandey et al. 2024
investigated the whole-atmosphere growth rate errors resulting from using MBL sites
and found the error to be 0.25 PgC per year (or 0.12 ppm per year) for the period 2015-
2019. This error includes stratosphere-troposphere exchange errors as well as within-
troposphere sampling errors.
An atmospheric inversion system produces the whole-atmosphere growth rate, which is
exactly equal to the sum of the fluxes added over a year. Inversion systems assimilate
the observations used to calculate the NOAA MBL growth rate. However, they also
represent 3D atmospheric transport using meteorological data. CAMS, for example,
assimilates the same NOAA flask data used to produce the NOAA MBL observations,
but it also accounts for vertical transport. The vertical gradients of these models are
validated using aircraft and satellite retrievals, explicitly resolve 3-D transport, and
include STE.
To address the reviewer’s concern, we validated the simulated model‑fraction field from
the CAMS inversion against in situ observations. Using the NOAA Marine Boundary
Layer Observation Network sites, CAMS reproduces the MBL CO₂ measurements with
high fidelity (SI Figure 7). This agreement demonstrates that CAMS not only employs
the same observational constraints as the NOAA MBL calculation but also accurately
matches them. As a full atmospheric inversion, CAMS also accounts for transport
processes such as stratosphere–troposphere exchange. To assess this, we compared
CAMS‑simulated CO₂ mixing‑ratio fields with independent AirCore observations. In
2016, observed stratospheric air-core profiles are 4-5 ppm lower than the tropospheric
average, and CAMS successfully captures this reduction (SI Figure 6) while also
matching the NOAA MBL observations well. In summary, CAMS captures the MBL CO2
growth rate and STE transport, and the integration of surface carbon fluxes over a year
from CAMS represents the carbon released to the whole atmosphere, thus, the
atmospheric CO2 growth rate based on CAMS is more accurate.
The box-model solution presented here is a simple parametric correction that accounts
only for stratosphere–troposphere exchange time. Its primary objective is to simulate
the CO₂ mixing ratio difference induced by this exchange. We provide an analytical
solution that can be readily applied to NOAA MBL growth rates, yielding a substantial
AGR correction and a corresponding reduction in the global carbon-budget imbalance.
The box model assumes an exchange time of 2 years, based on 80% of the
atmospheric mass residing in the troposphere. To validate this exchange time, we
compared the simulated stratosphere–troposphere CO₂ mixing ratio difference with
AirCore observations and CAMS-simulated 3D mole fraction fields. We extracted the
CAMS 3D mole fraction fields for 2016 and computed the annual mean CO₂ gradient
across the 200 hPa boundary (SI Figure 5). We found a stratosphere–troposphere CO₂
mixing ratio difference of 4–5 ppm in 2016, which is consistent with both CAMS and the
AirCore observations, confirming that our chosen exchange timescale for the 200 hPa
box is a reasonable estimate. Note that the CAMS mole-fraction fields have already
been validated against NOAA MBL as well as independent aircraft and air-core profiles.
Overall, the whole-atmospheric conversion error arises from well-understood physical
effects, the main one being the finite rate of STE. Because the STE bias arises from a
well-understood physical process that can be parameterized (box model) or explicitly
simulated (inverse models), we argue that these errors that can be corrected for using
established models.

Response: We agree with the reviewer that we expect the models to improve over time.
Our study seeks to move beyond this general intuition. Specifically, our objective is to
quantify the magnitude of these advancements and, to delineate the specific
components responsible for driving them. We believe our detailed investigation offers
distinct contributions:
1. Firstly, we introduce a quantitative benchmark for evaluating community-wide
progress. Through a comparative analysis of successive Global Carbon Project
(GCP) releases, we demonstrate a notable 16% reduction in the 1985–2016
RMS budget imbalance (from 0.91 to 0.76 Pg C yr⁻¹). To the best of our
knowledge, this constitutes the first objective, end-to-end metric for assessing
progress within the global carbon-budget modeling community.
2. Secondly, our research provides a component-level attribution of this observed
net gain. By propagating each updated term through our analytical framework,
we reveal that the improvements are not localized to a single component.
Instead, they are distributed across multiple elements, including the ocean sink,
land sink, land-use change emissions, atmospheric growth rate, and fossil-fuel
emissions.
3. Thirdly, in response to comments from Reviewer #3, we conducted an additional
experiment designed to determine whether the documented gains are
attributable to enhanced process realism or are merely statistical artifacts. Our
findings, derived from substituting the full ensemble of 20 DGVMs with a targeted
subset of six models that explicitly incorporate diffuse radiation effects, show a
further reduction in the RMS imbalance to 0.72 Pg C yr⁻¹. Conversely, a simple
expansion of the DGVM ensemble size from 15 to 20 models yielded no
discernible improvement. This suggests that the accurate representation of key
physical processes is a more critical determinant of model advancement than
sheer ensemble size.

Abstract:
"The Global Carbon Project (GCP) annually compiles an updated global carbon budget
that synthesizes state‑of‑the‑art estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions, land and
ocean sinks, and the atmospheric CO_2 growth rate. The residual between these terms,
referred to as the global carbon budget imbalance, reflects the aggregate inaccuracies
of the individual component estimates"
We have also modified the start of the introduction as per the suggestions of the
reviewer. First two paragraphs of the introduction:
“Accurate quantification of anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO_2) emissions and their
redistribution among Earth’s major carbon reservoirs (atmosphere, oceans, and
terrestrial biosphere) is essential for tracking mitigation progress, informing climate
policy, and projecting future climate trajectories (Schimel and Carroll 2024; Jones et al.
2023; Peters et al. 2017). As global temperatures rise and the impacts of climate
change intensify, the scientific community is refining observational and modelling tools
to constrain each component of the carbon cycle. The Paris Agreement’s five‑year
Global Stocktake further heightens this urgency by requiring transparent, robust
assessments of carbon sources and sinks to underpin effective policy‑making. Yet
persistent, poorly understood variability within the natural carbon cycle still hampers the
verification of reported emission reductions under international accords.
Over the past decade, researchers have addressed these shortcomings by acquiring
higher‑quality observations and activity data, expanding model ensembles, refining
parameterizations, and incorporating previously omitted processes—such as cement
carbonation and coupled nitrogen–phosphorus dynamics—into land and ocean carbon
models (Sitch et al. 2021; Xi et al. 2016; Hall et al. 2021; Friedlingstein et al. 2023).
These advances, which we collectively term “bottom‑up improvements”, improve the
process models (land and ocean uptake) and inventories (anthropogenic emissions)
that underpin contemporary carbon budgets. Although such improvements should, in
principle, reduce component‑level errors, unequivocal evidence of an overall gain in
accuracy remains elusive.”
Last paragraph of the introduction:
“Here, we investigate the evolution of collective accuracy using the carbon‑budget
imbalance reported annually by the Global Carbon Project (GCP). Specifically, we
quantify the error introduced when the MBL CO_2 growth rate is used as a proxy for the
global mean atmospheric growth rate. We find that accounting for the discrepancy
between MBL and whole‑atmosphere growth rates markedly reduces the
root‑mean‑square (RMS) of the annual imbalance time series relative to the values
reported in recent GCP Carbon Budget assessments. We further assess the impact of
updates to individual budget components between the 2017 and 2023 GCP reports,
demonstrating that the overall accuracy of Earth’s carbon‑budget components has
improved over this period.”
The article has two main sections. The first covers the improvement to the atmospheric
growth rate. The second part explores whether there have been improvements in other
terms in the carbon budget over time, as represented by their contribution to the carbon
budget imbalance. The comparative contribution provides useful context for each
section, though the analysis is mostly independent across the two main sections.

The carbon budget imbalance analysis presented here can serve as a diagnostic for
